source.title: RouterInterp: Understanding Superposed Specialisation in Mixture of Experts Routing
source.authors: I. Lasy; Nora Yinuo Cai; K. Ayonrinde

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the superposition idea to MoE routing in two language models and reports results on semantic diversity and routing prediction, rather than reproducing the original toy-network geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper tests whether MoE experts are associated with multiple semantically disjoint SAE features and whether SAE features predict routing. It does not test the original toy-model geometry, feature directions’ angles, or a sparsity-dependent geometric transition. Reported explanation scores and comparisons among explanation-generation methods are not included as claim rows; they primarily evaluate RouterInterp. Table 2's gpt-oss result is not duplicated because Table 3 reports the same layer-12 SAE predictor macro-F1.
record.test_reason: The paper mainly uses SAEs as a tool. Its matched-sparsity probe comparison (Table 2, Table 3) does bear on V4: on the same residual activations, SAE latents carry more routing-relevant structure than the neuron or PCA basis in two real MoE LLMs. The expert-level clustering and the m-sweep test the paper's own Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis about experts, not neuron-level superposition, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that experts are highly polysemantic (superposed specialisation, not domain specialisation) and that SAE features predict routing better than token statistics and matched-sparsity neuron/PCA probes. They also conclude that RouterInterp explanations beat baselines (0.49 / 0.60 vs 0.30 / 0.34). They note dependence on SAE quality (layer 16) and that only two models were evaluated.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes SAE features associated with MoE routing and semantic clustering; it does not reproduce the original toy-model training setup or its geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Routing-prediction strength varies by layer, SAE sparsity, and number of active SAE features retained; the paper reports weaker results at layer 16 and links probe performance to SAE reconstruction quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Each MoE expert's top-20 predictive SAE latents fall into many semantic clusters. The mean is 11.3 for gpt-oss-20b L20 and 10.8 for OLMoE L15, against 1 under the DSH prediction and about 16.6 under random assignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts are polysemantic at the routing level (superposed specialisation): each expert serves several semantically disjoint micro-domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Routing-prediction F1 rises as more active SAE features are kept per token (e.g., L20 from 0.280 at m=1 to 0.789 at m=128). Expert routing preferences across Pile subsets cluster near the corpus rate (Appendix D, Fig. 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE routing depends jointly on many fine-grained features rather than on one domain-level signal.

record.problems: Evidence concerns two MoE models and routing-related SAE features rather than general LLM representations; semantic clusters use generated latent explanations as proxies for micro-domains. The paper reports no uncertainty for the central cluster-count or routing-probe results, and acknowledges SAE reconstruction quality as a limitation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's individual neuron and PCA comparator values are represented as baselines rather than separate rows. Table 4's unigram and bigram comparator results are likewise listed as baselines. Table 2's gpt-oss-20b layer-12 SAE result duplicates Appendix E, Table 3. Explanation-score results in Sections 4.4 and Appendix H, and other RouterInterp method comparisons, were left out because they evaluate explanation performance or the method rather than directly measuring the claim's represented features.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature geometry, no sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features at the neuron level. The capacity idea is invoked only as motivation for expert routing.
No test of non-capacity causes of neuron polysemanticity.
Does not measure how features spread across neurons directly. The evidence is confined to router-relevant information in two MoE models. SAE completeness and exhaustiveness are not tested.
No test of SAE completeness, stability or canonicity.
No test of feature dimensionality. Multi-dimensional features are mentioned only as an SAE limitation.

missing.what: Pile-subset expert routing preference distribution (densities concentrated near 1). This is relevant to expert-level specialisation only.
SAE probe Spearman correlation with router probabilities by layer (0.258, 0.809, 0.741, 0.413, 0.817) and MSE of about 0.03.
missing.versions: V4 (weak; the SAE predictor's own fidelity, no basis comparison)

record.verdict_notes: The superposition analogy is applied to experts rather than neurons. Only the basis comparison bears on V4, and only indirectly. The m-sweep and cluster-count rows are reassigned to none. Table 4 rows at m=128 duplicate the Table 3 rows. No uncertainty is reported for the probe or cluster results.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-direction overlap or near-orthogonality measurements, or sparsity-dependent geometric transition are tested.
The study concerns MoE expert routing, not whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by limited representational capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE features associated with routing in two MoE language models; does not test feature distribution across neurons generally, other LLMs, or whether the identified SAE features are exhaustive.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Uses SAE latent directions but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of the underlying features.

rows.subject: gpt-oss-20b
rows.operation_detail: Clustered semantic explanations of each expert's top 20 predictive SAE latents; reported mean number of clusters per expert.
rows.measure: Mean semantic cluster count G(Ei) per expert
rows.baseline: DSH prediction: G=1; random assignment estimate: about 16.6 clusters among 20 latents and 50 equal-sized clusters
rows.note: The result is above the single-cluster prediction but below the n=20 upper bound and random-assignment estimate; the paper says this suggests some thematic coherence alongside multiple disjoint micro-domains.
rows.check: Counts semantic clusters among an expert's predictive SAE latents. This is polysemanticity of MoE experts/routing, not features superposed across neurons or dimensions. It is an analogous construct, so it is moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: OLMoE-1B-7B layer 11; gpt-oss-20b layers 4, 8, 12, 20 at s=64 and s=128
relationships.reason: At matched sparsity, SAE-basis probes beat neuron- and PCA-basis probes at predicting the linear router's choices. This indicates the SAE recovers sparse directions the model uses (r3–r6, r8–r11, r13).
relationships.display_finding: At matched sparsity, SAE-basis probes predicted the router's choices better than neuron- and PCA-basis probes, suggesting the SAE recovers sparse directions the model uses.

labels.reason: SAE recovery is weaker at layer 16 and loses its comparative advantage (r7, r12); Appendix G reports the highest FVU there. This qualifies the dictionary-based evidence without establishing absence of sparse features.

relation.reason: Although SAEs support its interpretation method, the study also compares learned SAE coordinates with neuron/PCA coordinates, bearing on V4.

tranche.reason: Matched-sparsity basis comparisons provide indirect evidence for recoverable sparse features in a new setting, real MoE routing; the study does not reproduce the original toy setup.

source_check.notes: Expert semantic-cluster counts measure expert-level polysemanticity, so r1/r2 correctly remain unlinked to the claim versions. Routing probes provide predictive evidence; they do not establish causal use of individual SAE features.

statements.correction: Appendices B/E: same residual activations, matched sparsity, neuron/PCA comparison controls for access to continuous residual representations; SAE wins at OLMoE layer 11 and gpt-oss layers 4/8/12/20, loses at layer 16. Appendix I: additional predictor validation against continuous router probabilities.
statements.problem: The routing comparison is accurate, but the blanket assertion of no reported controls overlooks the matched-sparsity, same-activation neuron/PCA comparisons.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OLMoE-1B-7B layer 11; gpt-oss-20b layers 4, 8, 12 and 20 in the matched-sparsity probe comparisons; and the reported multi-feature routing-prediction sweep
reader_labels.reason: SAE-based probes predict routing and often outperform matched alternatives; predictions improve substantially as more SAE features are retained (r3–r6, r8–r11, r13–r14, r18–r31, r35, r37, r39–r43). The semantic clustering results also find many clusters among predictive SAE latents per expert (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: gpt-oss-20b layer 16, and low-feature-count settings in several layers
reader_labels.reason: SAE-based prediction is weak at layer 16 and falls below the neuron probe there; with few active features, routing prediction is also substantially lower than with more features (r7, r12, r14–r17, r20–r22, r26–r27, r32–r34, r36, r38).
